full_judgment: 8. Mr. Amirul Kabir Chowdhury, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the State, submits that delay in disposal of the criminal case cannot be a ground for quashment of the criminal case. It is not disputed by him that there has been long delay in disposal of the case and the trial has not yet commenced and he further contends that an application for quashment of the proceeding was filed before the High Court Division earlier and the Rule issued in the case having been admittedly discharged no second revision for quashment of the same proceeding lies and hence the Rule is liable to be discharged. The learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that from the reading of the First Information Report and charge-sheet it cannot be said that the allegations contained therein do not disclose any offence and that the accused petitioners are not in any way connected with the commission of the offence alleged inasmuch as their names appear in the First Information Report with the allegation of their collaboration and connivance with the main accused Mostafa Anwar (since dead) and that being so, it cannot be said that there is no material for the prosecution of the accused petitioner. With regard to the revival of the case once stopped and consequent release of the accused on the expiry of the prescribed period of limitation the learned Deputy Attorney- General submits that it is within the jurisdiction of the court to revive a case invoking the aid of section 339D of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The learned Deputy Attorney-General, however, could not show any provision in the said section by which the court is vested with the power of revival of a case once stopped suo motu when such revival is not sought for by the Government or by the Public Prosecutor representing the State. Next point raised is as to whether the High Court has jurisdiction to quash the proceeding of a case in respect of which an application was filed earlier and the High Court refused to quash the proceeding is no doubt a debatable one. Mr. Amirul Kabir Chowdhury, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the State, strenuously contended that this application being a repetition of the same and similar prayer for quashment of the proceeding made in the application once rejected entertainment of the same application will tantamount to review of its earlier order by the High Court, which is outside the jurisdiction of High Court to do. He relied on two decisions of the Punjab and Orissa High Courts in support of his contention, namely Hoshear Singh Vs. The State, AIR 1988 Punjab 312 and Hamdeo Sudhi Vs. The State, AIR 1958 Orissa 20. The facts and circumstances of those cases being different we find that the cited decisions are of no help to him to support his contention. The question as to the scope and ambit of the inherent power of the High Court under section 561A vis-a-vis an earlier order made by it was not covered by these decisions. In the instant case the High Court has not been called upon to revise or review the earlier order made by it in its revisional jurisdiction. Here the suitation is wholly different. In the earlier order the High Court rejected the application for quashment on the ground that it was not desirable to interfere with the proceeding at that stage. But when it is found that a criminal case is dragged on for an unusually long period, the High Court has definitely the jurisdiction under the changed circumstances to entertain the second application to pass an appropriate order for securing the ends of justice. The above view of ours finds support from the decision in the case of Superintendent and Remembrancer of Legal Affairs, WB Vs.
